item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How the Mecca Agreement aims to manage US separation from Middle East
item.description:
How the Mecca Agreement aims to manage US separation from Middle East

Submitted by Ilya Roubanis on Thu, 08/13/2026 - 19:28
The pact is looking to seize ownership of the status quo that revisionist powers want to upend
Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan shakes hands with Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif as Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman looks on after signing a joint defence agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on 7 August 2026 (Handout/Turkish presidency's press office/AFP)
Off

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey was unexpected but hardly surprising.

Some have framed it as a Sunni alliance, with the role of the House of Saud as custodians of the two holy cities (Mecca and Medina), Pakistan as a nuclear-armed South Asian Islamic Republic, and Turkey’s Europe-adjacent muscular strand of political Islam. However, this agreement has little to do with religious sectarianism. 

The Mecca partners have far-reaching industrial, military, and diplomatic ties. The agreement, or the sum of already functioning bilateral partnerships, is not an alliance with a single command structure.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on 7 August by Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, attempts to consolidate three strong bilateral relationships into a single collective defence framework.

Pakistan and Saudi Arabia concluded a Mutual Defence Agreement on 17 September 2025. At the time, it was speculated that this would provide Riyadh with a nuclear defence umbrella, although this point remains intentionally ambiguous. The Mecca pact adds a Turkish annex.

“It was about time that regional agency takes shape,” says the Bahraini analyst, Abdullah Aljunaid.

“Put it this way: it’s not Islamic. It’s not about containing Iran either. It is there to prove that the region can produce its own security. You have three major players within the region: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey. What you need to look out for now is the geographical gaps between those three domains, all the way up to Syria.”

The militaries of all three states have deep ties. Islamabad and Ankara have a longstanding defence partnership. It is no secret that the Turkish industrial complex makes full use of Pakistani human resources in research and development: the Kaan fifth-generation fighter project employs about 200 Pakistani engineers. Riyadh has relied on Pakistani soldiers and pilots for decades, funded Islamabad’s nuclear programme, and has provided financial breathing space to Pakistan’s fragile economy.

'Put it this way: it’s not Islamic. It’s not about containing Iran either. It is there to prove that the region can produce its own security'

- Abdullah Aljunaid, Bahraini analyst

Turkey is not only a supplier of arms to Pakistan but has modular input in strategic platforms such as the JF-17 Block III multirole jet fighter, which uses an ASLPOD targeting pod and can be fitted with a MURAD AESA radar and Bozdogan short-range air-to-air missiles.

Over the last five years, Riyadh and Ankara have been forging a common worldview.

As noted by Aljenaid, Saudi-Turkish relations gained strategic depth in Syria, where cooperation was hailed by Washington.

At present, the partnership is gaining strategic significance, as Riyadh sees Ankara as a strategic partner in fulfilling the kingdom’s 2030 Vision, which calls for the localisation of 50 percent of total military expenditure, focusing on armed vehicles, missiles, loitering munitions, and drones.

In this context, Riyadh has found that Turkish companies such as Baykar and Aselsan are more willing to engage in technology transfer, joint production, and research. In sum, while this agreement is not an alliance, it is not shallow.

However, turning three bilateral partnerships into a single alliance is no simple matter. 

Why now?

According to Oral Toga, a senior researcher at the Centre for Iranian Studies in Ankara, the Mecca Agreement was negotiated over two years. Its scope predates the us-israeli war on Iran. However, the timing of the agreement certainly relates to the events unfolding around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

American security guarantees lost much of their thrust during the Hormuz crisis. As noted by former US ambassador to Qatar Patrick Theros, Washington’s attack on Iran turned the American umbrella into a liability.

Washington was unable or did not prioritise air defence cover for its partners in the Gulf, creating an additional challenge to the region’s security architecture. 

"The Saudis have understood that the Abraham Accords have been a security guarantee for Israel, not the kingdom,” notes Dr Yeghia Tashjian, of the Issam Fares Institute at the American University of Beirut.

The conclusion is that the Gulf’s defence architecture needs foundations in the region. In that respect, Qatar invested in its partnership with Turkey even before the 2025 Israeli raid on Doha. 

Riyadh and Abu Dhabi followed two distinct routes: the Emiratis doubled down in their partnership with Israel, with Israel installing the outward layers of its Iron Dome architecture in the Gulf.

Riyadh turned to its historical security partner, Pakistan, while incrementally building on its partnership with Turkey.

Destructive ambiguity

The question is: to what end does this agreement go?

According to the foremost expert in Turkish-Israeli relations at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, Dr Gallia Linderstrauss, while this pact is framed as exclusively defensive, it is meant to convey a message to Iran and Israel, perhaps also the UAE.

'Slowly and gradually, in the next one-two-three years, we will see America reducing its presence in the Gulf, and concentrating in the South China Sea'

- Air Marshal (Retd) Saeed Khan

The lack of clarity is whether this agreement is in fact an alliance. This begs testing, a process that can be destructive. An agreement is a statement of agency. An alliance is a joint perception of national security threats and implies unified command. We are nowhere closer to a regional alliance since 7 August.

Pakistani troops and pilots have repeatedly mobilised in Yemen under the Saudi banner. It is doubtful they would take action under a Pakistani banner and challenge the Emiratis head-on.

The withdrawal of more than $3.5bn of Emirati deposits from the Central Bank of Pakistan in April 2026 was a warning signal that Islamabad’s loyalty to Riyadh may come at a tangible cost.

The deployment of Pakistanis is not the same as the mobilisation of Pakistan. Islamabad has priorities, and its ultimate loyalty lies with Riyadh; still, Islamabad will strive to avoid a head-on collision.

When it comes to Iran, Islamabad also has priorities. As the Air Marshal (Retd) Saeed Muhammad Khan and former Pakistani ambassador to Syria underscores, Pakistan shares an extensive and rather unstable border with Iran, facing the common challenge of Baloch separatism.

“We have over 1,000km border with them and the common threat of the Baloch. Slowly and gradually, in the next one-two-three years, we will see America reducing its presence in the Gulf and concentrating in the South China Sea. Things could change dramatically,” Khan said.

Iran says it is not concerned by new 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement'
Read More »

Islamabad has little appetite for a direct confrontation with Tehran.

Similarly, it is doubtful that Ankara would take on the challenge of deploying in Yemen, risking a direct conflict with Tehran, with which it shares a Kurdish challenge. Even Riyadh would rather avoid feeding Shia-Sunni sectarianism.

This regional reluctance to feed sectarianism has been “battle-tested” during successive US-Israeli campaigns against Iran.

Will these three powers mobilise together against common threats? Under current circumstances, foes may be tempted to test this resolve. That can be dangerous.

There are common challenges, not least in the Red Sea.

Turkey’s Turksom Camp in Mogadishu is a major anchor for its power projection in the region.

Pakistan is complementing this presence, signing a military cooperation agreement with Somalia that facilitates the landing of an expeditionary force.

At the same time, Israel recognised Somaliland in December 2025; the United Arab Emirates is known to use the infrastructure of Bosaso port and airport for logistical purposes in its engagement in the Sudanese conflict. At times, there is a clear polarisation between status quo and revisionism, but it's never as neat as in the case of Nato.

Whether a common worldview translates into joint mobilisation is a question that depends on the convergence of several contextual variables.

All parties have a range of interests. Turkish-Emirati military-industrial cooperation is strong and growing. Pakistan still depends on remittance flows from 1.6 million Pakistanis residing in the UAE.

One should not expect Saudi Arabia to punish India for supplying Israel with military equipment when the need arises, as military analyst Kamal Alam notes.

Where do we go now

The Mecca agreement presents an ambiguous message. The three defence partnerships framed by the agreement remain distinct and compartmentalised. What is simmering is a polarisation between the status quo and revisionist powers.

In Ankara, Manama, Riyadh, and Beirut, the Emirati-Israeli alliance is seen as seeking to revise the security status quo, while Iran is seen as seeking to revise the status quo in the Strait of Hormuz. This polarisation is problematic, not least for Israel, which must also manage the ambiguity of the American commitment to the region. 

'From an Israeli perspective, normalisation between Israel and Saudi Arabia, if not harder, is at least a more distant reality'

- Gallia Lindenstrauss, Institute for National Security Studies 

Politics in this sense matters, and elections could make a difference.

According to Dr Gallia Lindenstrauss, expanding the Abraham Accords to include Saudi Arabia is now a greater challenge.

“From an Israeli perspective, normalisation between Israel and Saudi Arabia, if not harder, is at least a more distant reality. That is of concern because this is something that was a priority for Netanyahu.”

Whether by reference to Israel’s de facto security zones in Lebanon and Syria, or Kurdish-controlled regions in Iraq and Iran, what unites the Mecca signatories is a commitment to the status quo.

“All three signatories have backed central state authority where the UAE has backed sub-state actors: the Sudanese army against the RSF, Yemen’s recognised government against the STC, Somalia’s territorial integrity against Somaliland’s recognition," Toga of the Centre for Iranian Studies tells MEE.

"Riyadh no longer faces that network alone, and after the Yemen confrontation of late 2025, that is a meaningful change. But I would not overstate it.”

This observation is the point of departure, a foundational consensus among analysts in Islamabad, Ankara, and the Gulf. In that respect, the Mecca Agreement is a statement of intent to shield the territorial status quo even as the US withdraws from the region.

A bigger development may be further Chinese mediation. As noted by analyst Aljunaid, China is well positioned to broker an understanding between Iran and the Mecca signatories. The US is no longer seen as having convening power.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'Agility vs depth': How the Mecca pact stacks up against the UAE-Israel alliance
item.description:
'Agility vs depth': How the Mecca pact stacks up against the UAE-Israel alliance

Submitted by Sean Mathews on Thu, 08/13/2026 - 18:55
Israel and the UAE have transactional ties based on military and intelligence sharing, but the Mecca pact has political depth
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, left, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, centre, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif meet in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on 7 August 2026 (Handout/Turkish presidency's press office/AFP)
Off

This summer, a senior UAE diplomat, Lanna Nusseibeh, held consultations with a US ally in Europe. The meeting was unremarkable but informative because of the impression the European country's officials walked away with.

“The UAE is totally aligned with Israel. It’s crystal clear that the partnership has no limits,” a European official who was in the meeting told Middle East Eye.

That clarity contrasts with the questions swirling in corridors of power - from the US to Asia - about the Mecca Agreement, which unites Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan under a mutual defence pact that many see as rivalling the UAE-Israel partnership. 

Western and Arab officials are still trying to decipher just how aligned Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are, let alone whether they can back each other up in a hot conflict. 

For example, no sooner had the ink on the Mecca pact dried than the Houthis in Yemen attacked Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery. Pakistan and Turkey did not come to Riyadh’s defence against the Iran-aligned group.

In contrast, when the UAE came under attack from Iranian drones and missiles earlier this year, Israel dispatched Iron Dome air defence batteries to the Gulf state. Abu Dhabi also joined Israel in launching hundreds of strikes on Iran.

“Israel did the UAE a big solid during the war. Abu Dhabi is not going to forget that,” a US official told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity.

But there are key differences between the two blocs. Despite the UAE and Israel’s military cooperation, their relations are still kept behind closed doors.

"At first glance, the UAE-Israel bloc delivers more tangible gains for both parties, but the Mecca pact may ultimately resonate more broadly and less transactionally,” Theodore Singer, a former US intelligence officer, told Middle East Eye.

'The Mecca club can be expanded'

When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that he visited the UAE at the height of the war on Iran, Abu Dhabi moved to deny the official statement. To many, that awkward diplomacy underscored just how unpopular the alliance remains outside Israeli and American circles. 

'The UAE-Israel alliance is a political pact, but in reality, it’s the military and intelligence elements that define it”

- Ayham Kamel, geopolitical analyst

In contrast, the Mecca pact was celebrated in public. It was announced that Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan joined together for Friday prayer in the holiest city in Islam. 

The UAE and Israel have cooperated for decades. Their ties were given a public cloak in 2020 when Abu Dhabi officially recognised Israel under the Abraham Accords brokered by the US.

They are united by their animosity towards Iran on one side and the Muslim Brotherhood on the other. Abu Dhabi’s escalating rivalry with Saudi Arabia, which has refused to recognise Israel, could give the two another point of agreement.

The Abraham Accords have also solidified support in Washington for the UAE’s ruling Al-Nahyan family, even as the Emirates has hedged against the US with countries like China.  

But some analysts say the alliance between the UAE and Israel lacks depth. In some ways, the Mecca pact is its foil.

“The UAE-Israel alliance is a political pact, but in reality, it’s the military and intelligence elements that define it,” Ayham Kamel, a geopolitical advisor on the Middle East, told MEE, referring to the Abraham Accords.

“The Mecca pact’s foundation is military, but it carries a lot of political meaning,” Kamel added, noting the agreement’s supposed foundation on a Nato-like Article 5 defence commitment.

A lack of strategic depth is actually a physical reality for Israel and the UAE.

The latter is expanding a military base in Somaliland that some officials in the Horn of Africa tell MEE could be used by Israel, but Somaliland is recognised only by Israel.

Israel enjoys especially close ties with Greece. Both Israel and the UAE have growing military and economic ties with India and Ethiopia.

But there are only one million Emirati nationals and 10.2 million Israelis. Few of their neighbours want to partner with Israel. Distrust of Israel has only grown in the wider Muslim world as a result of Israel's war on Gaza, which the United Nations and dozens of human rights groups have deemed a genocide. 

“The UAE-Israeli cooperation is more agile and gets things done. The Mecca pact is going to move slowly and take time, but it has a public support base,” Kamel told MEE. “And the club can be expanded”.

On paper, at least, the Mecca pact is formidable.

'Different threat perceptions'

Turkey boasts the second-largest army in Nato, Saudi Arabia is the Arab world’s only G-20 economy, and Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim country.

Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have effectively been allies for decades. The kingdom provided financial support to Islamabad as it was acquiring a nuclear weapon. Pakistani pilots and officers have long filled the ranks of the kingdom’s military. In return, the Gulf state has provided a financial lifeline to Islamabad.

But the two face different threats. 

UAE and Israel established fund for joint defence acquisition, sources say
Read More »

Saudi Arabia generally sees Iran as a more serious threat. In 2015, Saudi Arabia allied with the UAE to fight against the Houthis in Yemen. Pakistan decided against military involvement. Its more cordial ties to Tehran have positioned it as a mediator.

Meanwhile, until a few years ago, Turkey and Saudi Arabia were at loggerheads over the Muslim Brotherhood. In Egypt, Saudi Arabia backed Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, who came to power in a coup that overthrew Egypt’s late president, Mohamed Morsi, who was democratically elected, and an ally of Erdogan

Ties between Riyadh and Ankara hit rock bottom in 2019 when Turkey leaked audio tapes exposing the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi at Saudi Arabia's embassy in Ankara. It is only recently that Turkey and Saudi Arabia have converged in hotspots like Syria and Sudan.

“The Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey alignment is more complex, given that each operates in different regional environments and their perceptions of threat also differ considerably. It will take a lot of energy, effort and political will for the three states to find a way of working together and finding interoperability,” Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow and Gulf expert at Chatham House, told MEE.

The war on Iran has only deepened ties between Israel and the UAE. MEE revealed in May that the two countries established a joint fund for defence acquisitions.

Quilliam called the Israeli-UAE bloc “more actionable”.

“The relationship has had time to bed in and has passed through many tests since the Abraham Accords were signed, and we have seen the two countries draw closer since the Israel-US war against Iran started,” he added.

Which alliance has better interoperability?

Turkey said on Thursday that its new allies will hold ‌joint exercises and deepen defence industry cooperation. The latter is a key goal for Ankara, which is pitching its drones and other weapons systems across the Middle East.

The US and Turkey are Nato allies, while Saudi Arabia has long relied on the US as its main weapons supplier. Pakistan and Turkey have co-produced small warships, known as corvettes, as well as the Kaan fighter jet. They are working to produce Turkish anti-tank missiles. Saudi Arabia wants a local defence industry.

'The UAE has primarily US-systems that are interoperable with Israeli systems'

- Elizabeth Dent, Washington Institute for Near East Studies

But deep integration could pose a challenge.

Pakistan’s main military supplier is China. Turkey wants to sell the Kaan fighter jet it is developing to Saudi Arabia, but the kingdom is eyeing the F-35.

US officials tell MEE that Riyadh is unlikely to buy both.

Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia cannot match the intensity of Israel's defence cooperation with the US. The former’s military advantage is written into US law. Israel is openly lobbying against Saudi Arabia acquiring F-35s.

“The Israelis have a broad defence industrial base, vast intelligence apparatus and battle-proven air and missile defence that is integrated via the US-led regional security order," Elizabeth Dent, a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and a former Pentagon official focused on the Gulf, told MEE.

“The UAE has primarily US systems that are interoperable with Israeli systems, and have the money and regional prowess,” she added.

Still, some analysts say that the very fact that Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have publicly codified their agreement gives it room to grow, potentially in ways the UAE-Israel alliance is unable to.

The Mecca pact "contains a lot more strategic depth and binding commitment on mutual defence which could ultimately provide a more credible deterrent,” Dent said. “But the countries aren’t already integrated, so they have a long way to go”.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israeli forces will not withdraw from south Lebanon or Gaza, Katz says
item.description:
Israeli forces will not withdraw from south Lebanon or Gaza, Katz says

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Wednesday that Israeli forces would not withdraw from what Israel calls its "security zones" in southern Lebanon or Gaza, in a video statement filmed from the Israeli-occupied Beaufort Ridge in Lebanon.

Katz's remarks came days after Israeli and Lebanese officials held talks in Rome on implementing a 26 June agreement linking Israel's phased withdrawal from southern Lebanon to the verified disarmament of Hezbollah.

Hezbollah, which is not a party to the agreement, has rejected calls to disarm. The US has since criticised Katz's remarks, saying they are inconsistent with Israel's commitments under the agreement.
